note: What this file is: chapter 2's narration (outline A, 'Back to the shell factory'), page by page, as it will be sent to ElevenLabs. Every page opens with the one accent instruction and has no other delivery cues; no capitals for emphasis; pauses written as '...'. Research ids for each sentence are in the script file '19 Script - chapter 2 - what really causes inflation.md'.
accent_instruction: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent]

pages.name: the question
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So... won't creating money just cause inflation? You've felt it at the checkout. The same basket of shopping costs more than it did a year ago. That's inflation... prices in general, going up. Not one price tag. The whole basket. To see what drives it, go back to the shell factory.

pages.name: back to the shell factory
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Britain, 1915. Fewer than one in a hundred people are out of work. The war is paid for partly with new money. And submarines are sinking ships full of food and materials. So more money is chasing fewer things to buy... and by the end of the war, prices have roughly doubled.

pages.name: two factories
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Now picture two factories. In the first, the machines stand idle, and workers wait at the gate. New money arrives... the workers go in, and more shells come out. The price tag barely moves. In the second, every machine is already running flat out. The same money arrives... but no more shells can be made. So buyers bid against each other, and the price tag climbs. Britain at war was the second factory. It had run out of workers, materials and machines.

pages.name: things you can't make more of in a hurry
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] And some things can't be made more of in a hurry... like homes. In 1915, workers poured into Glasgow for war work, and landlords tried to push rents up by a quarter. About twenty thousand households refused to pay. Within weeks, Parliament froze rents.

pages.name: test one: lots of new money, flat prices
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So let's test the rule. Japan, 2013. Its central bank, the bank that issues the yen, sets out to double the money it has created, in two years. If new money alone pushed prices up, they'd soar. They barely move... about half a percent a year. Britain's central bank created hundreds of billions of pounds. Its own study found the new money pushed up the prices of things people own, like shares... and the biggest gains went to the richest households.

pages.name: test two: when less is being made
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Germany, 1923. Prices are already rising fast. Then French and Belgian soldiers march into the Ruhr, Germany's coal and steel heartland. Workers down tools, and the government keeps paying them... with new money. By November, one US dollar costs more than four trillion marks. This time, new money really did push prices up... while less and less was being made.

pages.name: test three: costs, not spending
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Sometimes the cause isn't spending. It's costs. In 1973, with prices already climbing, the price of oil nearly quadrupled in three months, and everything made or moved with fuel got dearer. And here, now? Prices rose four point one percent in the year to June. Take fuel out... and it's two point nine.

pages.name: the honest edge
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So yes... creating money can push prices up, when it's spent where workers are already flat out, or on things we can't make more of in a hurry. In 2021, our unemployment hit a record low, and house prices jumped about thirty percent in a year. An independent review says the pandemic support was right at first... but too strong, for too long.

pages.name: who pays to fight it
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So what's the usual cure? Britain, 1920. The Bank of England pushes its interest rate up to seven percent. Loans cost more, and people spend less. Within a year, unemployment jumps from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten. Prices do fall... but people pay with their jobs. /məˈteɪi/ argues that was part of the point. With fewer jobs, workers can't ask for more.

pages.name: spent on what?
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Here, our central bank, the Reserve Bank, pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent to five and a half. Unemployment has climbed from three point two percent to five point six. And now, it's raising its interest rate again. So next time someone tells you creating money causes inflation... ask them. Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?
